worksheet.title: Follow the Steps
worksheet.subtitle: Run the algorithm to make a pattern
worksheet.learning_goal: I can follow the steps of an algorithm to make a pattern.

parts.title: Run the algorithm
parts.text: Follow the steps in order, one at a time, to fill the boxes. Each step tells you which shape to draw in the next box. Running the steps makes a pattern.

parts.title: Follow the steps
parts.prompt: Do each step in order and draw ● or ■ in the boxes above. Read box 1 first, then box 2, and so on.

parts.title: Read your result
parts.prompt: What shape is in box 6? Draw it or write its name.

parts.title: You try — keep the pattern
parts.prompt: What is the pattern called (● ■ ● ■ …)? If there were a box 7, what shape would go there? Tell how you know.

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: Running an algorithm means doing each step in order. The same steps always make the same result — here, a circle-square pattern.

parts.title: What this worksheet teaches
parts.text: Students follow a 6-step set of instructions in order to fill a row of boxes, making a circle-square pattern, then read and continue it. Following steps in order to build a result is running a plan. No coding experience needed.

parts.title: Before you start (no computer needed)
parts.text: No computer — paper and a pencil. You read each prompt aloud. Optional: cut the steps into cards so students can physically slide them into order before writing.

parts.title: How to lead it (about 20 minutes)
text: 1. Show them (you do). Read box 1, draw its shape; read box 2, draw its shape — one box at a time, in order.
2. Do one together. Fill the first few boxes together (circle, square, circle…).
3. Let them try. Students finish the row, then read and continue the pattern.

parts.title: Answer key (these are the verified correct answers)
text: Exercise 1 — boxes 1–6: circle, square, circle, square, circle, square. Exercise 2 — box 6 is a square.
Exercise 3 — the pattern is circle-square (an AB pattern); box 7 would be a circle, because the pattern repeats and box 6 ended on a square.
Why it works: each step runs in order and changes only its own box, so the row always comes out the same.

parts.title: If students get stuck — and ways to adjust
text: Watch for: skipping a box or doing them out of order. Read the boxes strictly 1, 2, 3…
Make it easier: point to each box as you read its step.
Make it harder: ask what box 8 would be and how they know.

parts.title: Ontario curriculum link (official wording)
text: C3.1 — solve problems and create computational representations of mathematical situations by writing and executing code, including code that involves sequential events.
In plain terms: students put step-by-step instructions in the right order to get a result.
C3.2 — read and alter existing code, including code that involves sequential events, and describe how changes to the code affect the outcomes.
In plain terms: students read a set of steps, change or reorder one, and explain what the change did.

parts.title: You'll know it worked when
parts.text: The child fills the row in order and continues the pattern correctly.
